The Trump administration is allowing sanctioned oil tankers to undergo a process to start legitimately shipping crude oil, according to US Energy Secretary Chris Wright. He says that “dozens” and perhaps even “hundreds” of tankers could benefit (the later seems an exaggeration).

Iraq says its oil exports have surged so far in October to near pre-war levels. According to the country's oil minister, Iraq has exported ~3.4m b/d on average so far this month, down marginally from ~3.7m b/d pre-war, and up from ~3m b/d in September and ~2.4m b/d in August.

With WTI rallying last week vs gasoline and diesel, simple refining margins (say the 3-2-1 WTI crack spread) have come down sharply, touching this morning a 3½-month low at ~$55 a barrel (it was ~$75 in early Sept).

At the start of the conflict, crude rallied because everyone feared the incoming crude shortage (i.e., production shut-in = real loss in barrels).

But as the conflict dragged on, we headed for the proverbial “wall” because of tightness in oil products. Then, in June, they signed the MOU, released 150 million bbls of floating storage, and temporarily resolved the crude issue, while the product issue remained unresolved.

Refining margins skyrocketed, and then everyone thought, “No, no, we have a product shortage.” It’s funny how price action can so easily change a human’s mind.

The 3-2-1 crack spread rallied, and at one point diesel cracks traded higher than crude itself. Great. Refineries made a lot of money, and people thought, “Yeah, we have enough crude, not enough products.”

But then the tanker attacks escalated, and tanker rates started jumping. Then China, after 3 months of not buying crude (exactly the timeframe we thought they could save the world), started buying crude.

Oops, tanker rates started to skyrocket. 

Why? Because now that China wants crude and all those damn tankers want to make the short transit in SOH for 3-4x the pay vs. a long-haul transit, why wouldn’t they?

So they had issues getting tankers to do the other routes, which pushed everything up.
Now those same refineries that benefited from absurd margins are losing money because tanker rates are too high! Oh no, poor refineries.

Asian and European refineries are now contemplating run-cuts because the landed price is negative, which means product tightness will worsen ahead of the winter heating-demand season. Diesel, already super short-supplied, has no room for refinery run-cuts, so prices have to move up again.

But as you can probably tell from what I’m writing so far, none of this is sustainable. Tanker owners, likely seeing this slowdown in demand, will lock in higher rates in other regions, which will cap tanker rates. 

Refineries in Asia and Europe will take advantage of this small dip in tanker rates to lock in whatever crude they can get, which is probably why you are starting to see crude benefit versus both refining margins and tanker rates.

The core of the dilemma from the start is that crude oil has higher storage levels than product storage. That’s not rocket science because crude can be stored for years while petroleum products have an expiration date.

But as you run down all the available crude oil in storage, crude oil will capture any value shift from the other segments. In this case, tanker rates have eaten into what would’ve been the crude value, so this phenomenon will continue over the coming months.

More notably, as we get closer to that operational minimum, crude will rally disproportionately compared with everything else. Again, it’s probably important to say this, but crude has always been the fundamental issue in this conflict.
